events.title: (Sold Out) Rebellion Talks: Booze, Taverns & Rowdy Rebels
events.address: 4709 Dundas St W, Etobicoke, ON, M9A 1A8
events.overview:
Learn the role Toronto's raucous taverns played in the political tensions leading up to the Rebellion of 1837. In the middle of the 1800s, taverns played a central role in political life. Montgomery’s Inn served as a watering hole during those tense years, making it the perfect place to discuss Toronto’s tavern history and how these places helped set the stage for Mackenzie’s attempted revolution.

From October 2026 to April 2027, historian Adam Bunch brings Toronto’s history to life in a series of talks exploring the Upper Canada Rebellion and its lasting impact on the city. From spies and taverns to political reform, rural rebels and the Patriot War, each talk reveals a different story connected to the museum where it takes place.

events.title: A Christmas Carol
events.place: The Fleck at Harbourfront Centre Theatre
events.address: 231 Queens Quay W, Toronto, ON, M5J 2G8
events.posterCredit: Sanjay Talwar as Ebenezer Scrooge, with the cast of A Christmas Carol (Travis… / City of Toronto
events.overview:
Dickens’s timeless holiday story of transformation, kindness and human connection.

This fresh adaptation by Tim Carroll brings Charles Dickens’s world to life through inventive puppetry, towering ghosts that fill the stage, traditional carols and audience participation with spirited sing-alongs. Interactive performers mingle throughout the theatre, while beautifully detailed period costumes and sets create an atmospheric Victorian Christmas.

More than 175 years after Dickens first published A Christmas Carol, audiences still recognize themselves in Ebenezer Scrooge: someone who discovers that it’s never too late in life to choose kindness and human connection. For centuries, this iconic story has endured because its themes are still relevant today: What really matters to us? And can people truly change?

events.title: Allan Gardens
events.overview: Allan Gardens is a public park and conservatory located in the Garden District of Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The property includes a playground, off-leash dog park, and a 1,500 square metres conservatory with six greenhouses. The park originated from lands donated to the Toronto Horticultural Society by George William Allan in 1858, with the horticultural society officially opening a gardens there in 1860. In 1864, the municipal government of Toronto acquired the lands surrounding the gardens, although it allowed the horticultural society to maintain it in return for permitting its public use.

events.title: Always In Fashion
events.overview:
Curated by Amber-Dawn Bear Robe, enjoy an immersive exploration of Indigenous design languages and their transformative impact on the fashion landscape of the lands we call Canada and the United States.

This exhibition emerges from the urgent need to recognize and celebrate Indigenous designers who are reshaping the industry by reclaiming cultural narratives, innovating with ancestral techniques, and challenging colonial frameworks within fashion.

Through research on Indigenous fashion history, cultural sustainability, and decolonial design practices, the exhibition highlights how contemporary Indigenous couturiers blend ancestral knowledge with cutting-edge innovation to redefine fashion on their own terms.

events.title: Back to Pompeii
events.address: 30 Hanover Rd, North York, ON, M3K 0E2
events.overview:
An immersive exhibition that invites guests to step inside ancient Pompeii.

Visitors can walk through a Pompeian house and city street, exploring spaces such as a bakery, a thermopolium (an ancient Roman commercial snack bar), a school, a tavern and baths. Guided by an original audio narrative, they can interact with everyday objects while discovering Roman water systems, medicine, food, fragrances and graffiti.

Highlights include The Earth Remembers, a 200-square-metre immersive room tracing the city’s history and the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, and a Walking VR journey (only available for ages 7 and up) through the ancient city, including its shops, amphitheatre and coastline.

events.title: Fort York
events.overview: Fort York is an early 19th-century military fortification in the Fort York neighbourhood of Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The fort housed members of the British and Canadian militaries and defended the entrance to Toronto Harbour. The fort features stone-lined earthwork walls and eight historical buildings within them, including two blockhouses. The fort forms a part of Fort York National Historic Site, a 16.6 ha site that includes the fort, Garrison Common, military cemeteries, and a visitor centre.

events.title: Geoffrey James | Ancient and Modern: Selected Panoramas
events.address: 1356 Dundas St W, Toronto, ON, M6J 1Y2
events.posterCredit: Near the Aqueduct Claudia, Rome (For Passolini), 1989 © Geoffrey James /… / City of Toronto
events.overview:
The Stephen Bulger Gallery is pleased to present there second solo exhibition of work by Geoffrey James, one of Canada’s pre-eminent photographers.

James’s panoramic photographs explore the relationship between people and the landscapes they create, shape, and transform. He became known for using a panoramic camera to photograph gardens, parks, cities, mines, and other human-made environments.

His photographs are carefully composed and largely devoid of people. His images of formal European gardens reveal the ways in which humans organize and control nature, while later photographs of places such as mines and borders explore the more destructive consequences of human intervention.

events.overview:
A joyful comedy that flips the script on Shakespeare's most infamous heroines.

To celebrate the 40th anniversary of her landmark play, acclaimed novelist and playwright Ann-Marie MacDonald steps into the spotlight as Constance Ledbelly, the overlooked academic who tumbles headlong into Shakespeare’s worlds and discovers that the heroines (and even Constance herself) may be capable of far more than anyone imagined.

At once wildly funny and moving, this Canadian classic unleashes Desdemona and Juliet as fierce forces of their own destiny and reminds us that sometimes the bravest act is claiming your own story.

events.overview:
The philosopher Diana Prokofyeva considers a photograph to be a phenomenon that exists as a way to avoid death by copying a moment and suspending it within time - a way to be between two worlds:, the living and the dead. She suggests that a photograph gives confidence of existence, a way to state, “Here I am and was, and always shall have been.”.

View this evolving series that looks to photography as a method of conceptualizing grief and mortality. Using family archives from the past century and conceptual imagery, I locate myself within a chain of human experience. I look to the women who came before me, observing the proof of their existence with reverence and the knowledge that I will one day add to this catalogue. Through this series I aim to overshadow existential fear with curiosity.

events.overview: Step into the intricate world of artist David Currie as he explores how humans are hard-wired to seek out patterns as a means of adapting to their environment, whether connecting imaginary lines to stars or writing algorithms that direct a robot’s movements. stops.title: CN Tower
stops.text: The CN Tower is a 553.3-metre-high communications and observation tower in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Completed in 1976, it is located in downtown Toronto, built on the former Railway Lands. Its name "CN" refers to Canadian National, the railway company that built the tower. Following the railway's decision to divest non-core freight railway assets prior to the company's privatization in 1995, it transferred the tower to the Canada Lands Company, a federal Crown corporation responsible for the government's real estate portfolio. The CN Tower held the record for the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years, from 1975 until 2007, when it was surpassed by the Burj Khalifa, and was the world's tallest tower until 2009 when it was surpassed by the Canton Tower.

stops.title: Greater Toronto Area
stops.text: The Greater Toronto Area, commonly referred to as the GTA, includes Canada's most populous city, Toronto, and the regional municipalities of Durham, Halton, Peel, and York. In total, the region contains 25 urban, suburban, and rural municipalities. The Greater Toronto Area begins in Burlington in Halton Region to the west, and extends along Lake Ontario past downtown Toronto eastward to Clarington in Durham Region. According to the 2021 census, the Census Metropolitan Area of Toronto has a total population of 6.202 million residents, making it Canada's most populous metropolitan area, and the 7th-largest in North America. However, the Greater Toronto Area, which is an economic area defined by the Government of Ontario, includes communities that are not included in the CMA, as defined by Statistics Canada.

stops.title: Toronto-Dominion Centre
stops.text: The Toronto-Dominion Centre, or TD Centre, is a skyscraper complex in the Financial District of downtown Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Owned by Cadillac Fairview, it is the global headquarters for its anchor tenant, the Toronto-Dominion Bank, and provides office and retail space for many other businesses. The complex consists of six towers and a pavilion covered in bronze-tinted glass and black-painted steel. Approximately 21,000 people work in the complex, making it the largest commercial office complex in Canada. The project was the inspiration of Allen Lambert, former president and chairman of the board of the Toronto-Dominion Bank.

stops.title: The St. Regis Toronto
stops.text: The St. Regis Toronto is a mixed-use skyscraper located in the downtown core of Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It was built by Markham-based Talon International Development Inc., which is owned by Canadian businessmen Val Levitan and Alex Shnaider. The hotel portion of the building is owned by InnVest Hotels LP, which acquired it in 2017. The building is located in Toronto's Financial District, at 325 Bay Street, on the southeast corner of Bay and Adelaide streets.

stops.title: Hockey Hall of Fame
stops.text: The Hockey Hall of Fame is a museum and hall of fame located in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Dedicated to the history of ice hockey, it holds exhibits about players, teams, National Hockey League records, memorabilia and NHL trophies, including the Stanley Cup. Founded in Kingston, Ontario, the Hockey Hall of Fame was established in 1943 under the leadership of James T. Sutherland. The first class of honoured members was inducted in 1945, before the Hall of Fame had a permanent location. It moved to Toronto in 1958 after the NHL withdrew its support for the International Hockey Hall of Fame in Kingston, Ontario, due to funding issues.

stops.text: St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica is the cathedral church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Toronto, Canada, and one of the oldest churches in Toronto. It is located at 65 Bond Street in Toronto's Garden District. St. Michael's was designed by William Thomas, designer of eight other churches in the city, and was primarily financed by Irish immigrants who resided in the area.

stops.title: Yonge Dundas Square
stops.text: Sankofa Square, colloquially Dundas Square, is a public square and outdoor venue at the southeast corner of the intersection of Yonge Street and Dundas Street East within the Garden District in the downtown core of Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The square was conceived in 1997 as part of a revitalization of the intersection and the stretch of Yonge Street. Since its completion in 2002, the square has held many public events, performances and art displays, establishing itself as a prominent landmark in Toronto and one of the city's prime tourist attractions. Surrounding the square are other major landmarks, including the Toronto Eaton Centre, Ed Mirvish Theatre, and the 33 Dundas Street East building. The square is accessible from the Toronto subway at TMU station and is connected to Path, Toronto's underground pedestrian walkway.

stops.title: Art Gallery of Ontario
stops.text: The Art Gallery of Ontario is an art museum in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Located on Dundas Street West in the Grange Park neighbourhood of downtown Toronto, the museum complex takes up 45,000 square metres of physical space, making it one of the largest art museums in North America and the second-largest art museum in Toronto, after the Royal Ontario Museum. In addition to exhibition spaces, the museum also houses an artist-in-residence office and studio, dining facilities, event spaces, gift shop, library and archives, theatre and lecture hall, research centre, and a workshop. Established in 1900 as the Art Museum of Toronto and formally incorporated in 1903, the museum was renamed the Art Gallery of Toronto in 1919, before adopting its present name, the Art Gallery of Ontario, in 1966. stops.title: Royal Ontario Museum
stops.text: The Royal Ontario Museum is a museum of art, world culture and natural history in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It is one of the largest museums in North America and the largest museum in Canada. It attracts more than one million visitors every year, making it the most-visited museum in Canada. The 74,000-square-metre museum building is located north of Queen's Park, in the University district, with its main entrance on Bloor Street West. Museum subway station is named after it and, since a 2008 renovation, is decorated to resemble the ROM's collection at the platform level; Museum station's northwestern entrance directly serves the museum.

stops.text: The Bata Shoe Museum is a museum of footwear and calceology in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The 3,665-square-metre museum building was designed by Moriyama & Teshima Architects, with Raymond Moriyama as the lead architect. stops.title: Coca-Cola Coliseum
stops.text: Coca-Cola Coliseum is an arena at Exhibition Place in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, used for agricultural displays, ice hockey, basketball, and trade shows. It was built for the Canadian National Exhibition and the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair in 1921. Since 1997, it has been part of the Enercare Centre exhibition complex. It serves as the home arena of the Toronto Sceptres of the Professional Women's Hockey League and the American Hockey League's Toronto Marlies, the farm team of the Toronto Maple Leafs. It also serves as the home arena of the Toronto Tempo of the Women's National Basketball Association since their debut in 2026.

stops.title: Exhibition Place
stops.text: Exhibition Place is a publicly owned mixed-use district in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, located by the shoreline of Lake Ontario, just west of downtown. The 197-acre site includes exhibit, trade, and banquet centres, theatre and music buildings, monuments, parkland, sports facilities, and a number of civic, provincial, and national historic sites. The district's facilities are used year-round for exhibitions, trade shows, public and private functions, and sporting events. From mid-August through Labour Day each year, the Canadian National Exhibition, from which the name Exhibition Place is derived, is held on the grounds. During the CNE, Exhibition Place encompasses 260 acres, expanding to include nearby parks and parking lots.

events.title: Distance to Independence - Documentary Screening
events.overview:
Discover a lesser-known chapter of Canadian history celebrating democracy and solidarity at a special documentary screening.

In 1991, approximately 80 young Canadians and Americans of Ukrainian descent, including many participants from Toronto, travelled to Ukraine to support its independence movement ahead of the December 1 referendum.

Through rare archival footage and firsthand accounts, the documentary explores Canadian civic engagement, international solidarity and the power of individuals to advance democracy. On December 2, 1991, Canada became the first Western country to recognize Ukraine's independence. Thirty-five years later, the film highlights Toronto's connections to global history as Ukraine continues to defend its sovereignty.

Join us on November 18 for a story of courage and civic responsibility, followed by a discussion and Q&A with the filmmakers.

events.overview:

Critically acclaimed by The New York Times, this breakthrough work from the writing team of composer David T. Little (Soldier Songs, JFK) and Canadian librettist Royce Vavrek (Angel’s Bone, Listen, Quiet) put them on the map. They have since gone on, both together and in collaboration with others, to revolutionize opera in North America.

events.title: Out of Line: 150 Years of Supporting Creative Defiance at OCAD U
events.posterCredit: Ginette Legaré: Jury Pool / City of Toronto
events.overview:
The Student Galleries mark OCAD University’s 150th anniversary with a pointed declaration of purpose by positioning the institution not merely as a site of technical training or aesthetic refinement, but rather as a long-standing incubator of creative disruption.

The exhibition gathers notable alumni and long-time faculty whose practices embody this refusal. These artists do not form a school or style, but rather what binds them is a shared willingness to step across boundaries, to trouble conventions and to keep culture unsettled in the interest of possibility.

The exhibition is both celebration and summons: a recognition of what has been achieved and an invitation to keep the boundaries moving.

events.title: (Sold Out) Rebellion Talks: The Strange & Tragic Tale of Robert Baldwin
events.overview:
Listen to the story of Robert Baldwin, one of the strangest and most pivotal figures in Canadian history. Not everyone who demanded change believed in violence. One of the leading champions of Canadian democracy refused to take up arms and join the rebels. Baldwin's summer home was located where the museum is today. Investigate the role Baldwin played in trying to find a peaceful solution to the rebellion crisis, how he eventually accomplished what Mackenzie never did, and the bizarre twist to his tragic love story.

From October 2026 to April 2027, historian Adam Bunch brings Toronto’s history to life in a series of talks exploring the Upper Canada Rebellion and its lasting impact on the city. From spies and taverns to political reform, rural rebels and the Patriot War, each talk reveals a different story connected to the museum where it takes place.

events.title: Curator’s Talk: Time, Labour and the Value of Beads
events.address: 327 Bloor St W, Toronto, ON, M5S 1W7
events.posterCredit: Bata Shoe Museum / City of Toronto
events.overview:
Beads may be small and intricate, but their histories reveal powerful stories of identity, value, and status.

In celebration of Brilliant: The Art of Beaded Footwear Around the World, join Director and Senior Curator Elizabeth Semmelhack for an informative and illuminating exploration of beadwork traditions from around the world and their role as markers of wealth, prestige, and cultural meaning.

From royal adornment and ceremonial regalia to trade and personal expression, this lecture traces how beads have signaled belonging across time and place. At its core is the labour behind the work: the skilled craftsmanship, generational knowledge, and cultural practices embedded in every stitch.

By centering time and labour, the talk challenges conventional ideas of value and asks what makes something “luxurious,” and who defines luxury.

events.title: Symposium: A Black History of Photography
events.overview:
Join us for a day of talks by international scholars and artists examining photography through the lens of Black history and experience.

From the invention of photography, Black populations across the globe have been at the forefront of the technology’s innovation and social use.

For many Black people living in the 19th and 20th centuries, photography served as a source of income, a platform for community building and political mobilization and as a component of everyday interaction. Black use and innovation of the medium have long unfolded beyond the gaze and support of Western fine arts museums and universities.

The history of photography is littered with universalisms that fail to capture the complex and diverse networks of circulation and innovation adopted by Black people.

events.address: 189 Yonge St, Toronto, ON M5B 1M4, Canada
events.overview:
A journey into the realm of memory.

Lepage plunges into the depths of memory and questions the relevance of certain recollections. Why do we remember the phone number from our youth, yet forget our current one? How does a childhood song withstand the test of time, while the name of a loved one escapes us? Why does meaningless information stay with us, while other, more useful information falls away?

The show considers various commemorative markers and the historical heritage around us that we no longer notice. The play also focuses on oblivion, the unconscious and memory that fades over time, whose limits are now compensated for by digital storage, mountains of data and virtual memory.

Somewhere between theatre performance and conference, Lepage reveals the suffering of an actor who must remember not only his text, but also his past, as well as the historical and social realities…

events.overview:

Composed in a prisoner-of-war camp during the Second World War, the work stands as one of the 20th century’s most profound musical testaments of faith, transcendence and human resilience.

Twenty-five years and countless performances later, the Gryphon Trio and Campbell return to this monumental masterpiece that has become a defining thread in their artistic story. The program opens with the stormy passion of Johannes Brahms’ dramatic Piano Trio in C minor and also features the world premiere of a new work for piano trio by Graham Campbell.

events.address: 67 Pottery Rd, East York, ON, M4K 2B9
events.overview:
Learn about the violent aftermath of the Rebellion of 1837. The revolutionaries didn't give up easily. Even after Mackenzie's army was crushed at the Battle of Montgomery's Tavern, the rebels kept fighting. They rallied new supporters as they seized control of an island in the Niagara River, declared it to be the independent Republic of Canada, and launched what became known as the Patriot War. It's a story of bloody battles, revolutionary spies, pirate admirals, and two competing visions for the future of the continent.

From October 2026 to April 2027, historian Adam Bunch brings Toronto’s history to life in a series of talks exploring the Upper Canada Rebellion and its lasting impact on the city. From spies and taverns to political reform, rural rebels and the Patriot War, each talk reveals a different story connected to the museum where it takes place.

events.title: Canadian Premiere: A German Life
events.overview:
Complicity rarely announces itself.

From Tony- and Oscar-winning writer Christopher Hampton and based on the real-life testimony of Brunhilde Pomsel, secretary to Joseph Goebbels in 1940s Germany, A German Life traces one woman’s extraordinary life inside a regime built on propaganda and terror.

At the age of 103, Pomsel looks back and recounts her work, her choices and her daily survival. Hampton’s adaptation examines the incremental slide – the quiet rationalizations and small concessions through which ordinary people become entangled in extraordinary evil.

A German Life is a meditation on memory, guilt and the fragile line between complicity and innocence.

The play, directed by Stewart Arnott, stars Canadian theatre legend Fiona Reid, whose work has been seen across the country at Stratford, Shaw and beyond, including on film, in My Big Fat Greek Wedding and The Time Traveler’s…

events.title: Sex in the '80s
events.posterCredit: Kate Hennig, Oliver Dennis, Jacob MacInnis and Heeyun Park. Photos by Dahliz… / City of Toronto
events.overview:
Old history. New rules.

They haven’t seen each other since the 1980s. Now two accomplished architects are reunited in a glass-walled Toronto office tower on the eve of a high-stakes competition. Both intend to keep things strictly professional. That proves harder than expected.

As a long-buried chapter of their shared history resurfaces, a polite reunion turns into a pointed, funny sparring match about memory, ambition, and how much the rules have changed. Meanwhile, their twentysomething colleagues look on and aren’t shy about weighing in.

Smart, topical, and wickedly witty, this is a workplace comedy about generational change and the risky business of revisiting the past.

events.title: Bouchara: The Light of Other Worlds
events.address: 273 Bloor St W, Toronto, ON M5S 1W2
events.overview:
Brian Current leads Glenn Gould School students in bold contemporary music that opens imagined worlds. Enjoy pieces from Claude Vivier’s Bouchara to works by Hannah Kendall and Francis Battah.

Bouchara, Vivier’s luminous work for soprano and ensemble, is widely recognized as one of his most beautiful and singular creations. Sung in an invented, intimate language, it opens a sound world that feels both ancient and deeply personal.

Alongside it, shouting forever into the receiver by Hannah Kendall, one of today’s most compelling international voices, and Francis Battah’s Musique d’un monde sans carte, extend this sense of hidden worlds: places we cannot quite name, where sound becomes a space of memory, imagination and discovery.

events.title: Fire Building with Kory Snache

events.overview:

Join us as we learn about Anishnaabeg general understanding of fire and how to create a fire in all seasons. Participants will get to go outside and gather material and try various ways in which to start a fire.

We acknowledge that Downsview Park is on the traditional territory of many nations including the Mississaugas of the Credit, the Anishnabeg, the Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee and the Wendat peoples and is now home to many diverse First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples. We also acknowledge that Toronto is covered by Treaty 13 signed with the Mississaugas of the Credit.

events.overview:

Widely hailed as the first masterpiece of the 21st century, Georg Friedrich Haas’s in vain is one of the most admired works of our time.

Performed by a group of Toronto’s top professional musicians, this extraordinary piece transforms sound into a living, shifting landscape of microtonal colour. At its centre is a breathtaking 20-minute passage where the audience is plunged into total blackout.

events.overview:
Learn about the riots that shook Toronto to its core in the years before and after the Rebellion of 1837 in the rebel mayor’s former home, which is now Mackenzie House Museum. Political violence was a common occurrence in Toronto; rival factions battled in our streets. Hear the history behind the riots that helped convince Mackenzie that an armed revolution was his only option and explore the riots that continued to rage long after his rebellion was over.

From October 2026 to April 2027, historian Adam Bunch brings Toronto’s history to life in a series of talks exploring the Upper Canada Rebellion and its lasting impact on the city. Few musicals feel as essential to revisit or as urgent to re-examine as Cabaret.

Set in Berlin as the shadows of extremism lengthen, Cabaret invites us into a world of music, seduction and dangerous denial. Beneath its unforgettable songs lies one of musical theatre’s most incisive examinations of how societies unravel. Not overnight, but slowly, and in plain sight.

Nadja Lubiw-Hazard examines trauma, grief, healing and connection through characters including a veterinarian, a grieving mother and a woman reflecting on Chernobyl's feral dogs, revealing how all living beings are linked.
